p: In the early seventh century after Christ, the two great powers of the civilised West were the Roman Empire of Constantinople and the Persian Empire of the Sasanian kings, and they had just fought one another, for a quarter of a century, to a state of mutual exhaustion. To the south of them lay Arabia, a land of deserts and oases, of nomadic tribes and trading towns, which neither empire had thought worth conquering. Within a generation, the armies of a new faith that arose in Arabia had destroyed the Persian Empire entirely and stripped Constantinople of Syria, Palestine and Egypt. Within a century, they ruled from Spain to the borders of India. No event in history, save perhaps the conquests of the Mongols, was so swift or so unexpected, and none has been more lasting.

Muhammad was born in the trading town of Mecca, in western Arabia, about the year five hundred and seventy, into the clan of Hashim of the powerful tribe of Quraysh. He was orphaned young and raised by his grandfather and his uncle. As a young man he worked in the caravan trade and earned a reputation for honesty; he married a wealthy widow, Khadija, who employed him, and who was his only wife for twenty-five years, until her death. Mecca was a centre of pilgrimage to a shrine called the Kaaba, which housed the images of many gods, and the Quraysh profited from the pilgrims.

About the year six hundred and ten, according to Muslim tradition, Muhammad, who was in the habit of retreating to a cave on a mountain near Mecca to meditate, received a revelation through the angel Gabriel, commanding him to recite. These revelations continued for the rest of his life, and were gathered after his death into the Quran, a word meaning the recitation. He preached that there is no god but the one God, Allah in Arabic, the same God whom the Jews and Christians worship; that he, Muhammad, was the last of a line of prophets including Abraham, Moses and Jesus; that all would face a Day of Judgement; and that the rich must care for the poor, the orphan and the widow. The word Islam means submission, that is, to the will of God, and a Muslim is one who submits.

This message threatened the gods of Mecca and the trade that depended on them, and the leading men of the Quraysh persecuted the small community of his followers. In six hundred and twenty-two, Muhammad and his followers emigrated to the oasis town of Yathrib, some two hundred miles to the north, whose quarrelling tribes had invited him to come as an arbitrator. The town became known as Medina, the city of the Prophet, and the emigration, called the Hijra, marks the first year of the Muslim calendar. At Medina Muhammad became not only a prophet but a statesman, lawgiver and general. After years of war with Mecca, he entered it in six hundred and thirty almost without bloodshed, destroyed the idols of the Kaaba, and dedicated it to the worship of the one God. By his death in six hundred and thirty-two, most of Arabia had accepted his rule.

I have given the account as the Muslim tradition gives it, and as the Encyclopaedia reports it, with the caution that our sources were written down a century or more after his death. The historian will note that few founders of religions have so shaped not only the beliefs but the laws, the politics and the daily habits of their followers: prayer five times daily, facing Mecca; the fast of the month of Ramadan; alms for the poor; and the pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime, which has brought together, every year for fourteen centuries, believers from every nation and of every colour, in the same plain white garments.

After the Prophet's death, his successors, called caliphs, a word meaning deputy or successor, led the Arabs out of Arabia. At the river Yarmuk in Syria, in six hundred and thirty-six, they defeated the army of Constantinople; at Qadisiyya in Iraq, about the same time, the army of Persia. Jerusalem surrendered in six hundred and thirty-seven, and the caliph Umar entered it on foot, by the traditional account, and guaranteed the safety of its Christian inhabitants and their churches. Egypt fell by six hundred and forty-two, Persia was wholly conquered within a few years more, and the advance went on, across North Africa and into Spain in seven hundred and eleven, and across Central Asia to the borders of China. In seven hundred and thirty-two, an Arab raiding army was turned back near Tours, in the heart of France, by Charles Martel, grandfather of Charlemagne. Gibbon remarked, with his usual irony, that but for that battle, the Quran might now be taught in the schools of Oxford. That is an exaggeration; the raid was not an invasion. But the advance of Islam into Western Europe did stop there.

The conquests are explained in part by the exhaustion of the two empires, in part by the zeal and the hardihood of the Arab armies, and in part by the fact that many of the conquered had little love for their former masters. The Christians of Syria and Egypt, whose doctrines Constantinople regarded as heretical and had persecuted, often found Arab rule easier to bear. The conquerors did not, in the first centuries, generally force conversion; Jews and Christians, as peoples of the book, were allowed to keep their faith on payment of a special tax. Conversion came slowly, over centuries.

The unity of the faith did not last long. A dispute over who should succeed the Prophet, between those who followed the elected caliphs and those who held that the leadership belonged to the family of Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, led to civil war and to the lasting division between the Sunni and the Shia, which persists to this day and to the day of the Encyclopaedia. But the civilisation that arose from these conquests, with its capital at Damascus and then at Baghdad, became for some centuries the most learned, the most prosperous and the most refined in the western half of the world. Of that I shall speak next.
